clientProfiles.name: Daniel Ortiz
clientProfiles.summary: A married father of two young children whose income supports the household. He has only a small group life benefit through work and a tight budget.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Spouse (stays home with the children), children ages 2 and 5

facts.label: Existing coverage and savings
facts.value: $70,000 group term life through work; $15,000 savings

clientProfiles.goal: Make sure his family could keep the house, pay the bills and eventually fund the children's education if he died.

decisions.prompt: Which type of coverage best fits Daniel's need and budget?

options.text: A level term policy lasting until the youngest child is grown (about 20 years)
options.feedback: Term gives the most death benefit per premium dollar for a large, temporary need. A convertible term policy also keeps the option to move to permanent coverage later.

options.text: A whole life policy for the same face amount
options.feedback: Whole life for a large face amount would cost far more than $60 a month, so Daniel would end up badly underinsured or unable to keep paying.

options.text: A small whole life policy plus a term policy for the rest of the need
options.feedback: A blend can work if the total premium fits the budget, but most of the protection should come from term so the need is fully covered.

options.text: Rely on the $70,000 group life benefit
options.feedback: Group coverage is far below the family's needs and usually ends or must be converted if he leaves his job.

decisions.prompt: Using a needs approach, roughly how much coverage should Daniel consider for lump-sum needs alone? (Final expenses $15,000 + mortgage $240,000 + car loan $10,000 + education fund $100,000; subtract $70,000 group life and $15,000 savings.)

options.text: About $280,000 for lump-sum needs, plus more for ongoing income needs
options.feedback: $15,000 + $240,000 + $10,000 + $100,000 = $365,000. Subtracting $85,000 of existing resources leaves $280,000 — before adding income for the spouse during the dependency years.
That is the total of lump-sum needs, but it ignores the $85,000 of existing coverage and savings the family already has.

options.text: $70,000, the same as his group life
options.feedback: That simply duplicates existing coverage and leaves the mortgage and education needs unfunded.

options.text: Ten times his salary, without looking at his family's needs
options.feedback: A rule of thumb can be a starting point, but the needs approach looks at this family's actual debts, goals and resources.

decisions.prompt: Which rider is most worth discussing with Daniel?

options.text: Waiver of premium, so the policy stays in force if he becomes totally disabled
options.feedback: Daniel's family depends on his income; if a disability stopped his paycheck, waiver of premium would keep the coverage in force.

options.text: A children's term rider for small amounts on the children
options.feedback: Inexpensive and can cover final expenses for a child, but it addresses a much smaller risk than protecting Daniel's income.

options.text: An accidental death benefit instead of more base coverage
options.feedback: Accidental death pays only for accidents; Daniel's family needs protection from death by any cause, especially illness.

decisions.prompt: Daniel's spouse does not earn income. What should the producer point out?

options.text: Consider modest coverage on the spouse, since replacing child care and household work would cost money
options.feedback: The death of a stay-at-home parent creates real expenses. Survivor protection is not only for wage earners.

options.text: No coverage is needed on a spouse without a paycheck
options.feedback: That ignores the economic value of a stay-at-home parent's work.

options.text: Insure the spouse for the same amount as Daniel
options.feedback: Some coverage makes sense, but the amount should be based on the spouse's own needs analysis, not simply matched.

takeaways: Large, temporary needs on a tight budget usually point to term insurance, often convertible.
The needs approach totals lump-sum and income needs and subtracts existing coverage and savings.
Waiver of premium protects coverage when the insured's income stops because of disability.
Stay-at-home parents have an insurable economic value too.

clientProfiles.name: Aisha Bello
clientProfiles.summary: A single nurse with no dependents. Her parents co-signed $40,000 of her private student loans.

facts.label: Debts
facts.value: $40,000 private student loans co-signed by her parents

facts.label: Existing coverage
facts.value: $65,000 group term life through her hospital

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Expects to marry and have children within 5–10 years

clientProfiles.goal: Make sure her parents would not be stuck with her student loans if she died, and keep options open for future family needs.

decisions.prompt: How large is Aisha's current life insurance need?

options.text: Modest — enough to cover the co-signed loans and final expenses, beyond what she already has
options.feedback: With no dependents, her main exposure is the co-signed debt and final expenses. A needs approach keeps the recommendation proportionate.

options.text: A very large policy sized to ten times her salary
options.feedback: She has no one who depends on her income today, so a huge face amount is not supported by her needs.

options.text: None at all, because she is single
options.feedback: Her group life might cover the loans today, but it may end if she changes jobs; the co-signed debt still deserves attention.

decisions.prompt: Which feature best protects her future insurability as her family grows?

options.text: Convertible term, or a guaranteed insurability rider on a permanent policy
options.feedback: Conversion or guaranteed insurability lets her add or keep coverage later without new evidence of insurability, even if her health changes.

options.text: Relying only on group life from her current job
options.feedback: Group coverage depends on employment and is rarely enough once a family arrives.

options.text: Buying the cheapest one-year term policy and reapplying every year
options.feedback: It is inexpensive now, but each new application requires insurability and the price rises with age.

decisions.prompt: Aisha asks whether a policy with cash value is a good idea. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain the trade-offs: permanent coverage builds cash value but costs more; recommend it only if it fits her goals and budget
options.feedback: A balanced explanation of favorable and unfavorable features lets her make an informed choice.

options.text: Tell her cash value policies always beat term
options.feedback: No product is always best; cost, goals and time horizon matter.

options.text: Tell her term is always best for everyone
options.feedback: Permanent coverage can fit people with lifelong needs or a desire for cash accumulation; blanket statements are not sound advice.

takeaways: Without dependents, the need is usually limited to debts others would owe and final expenses.
Conversion privileges and guaranteed insurability protect future insurability.
Present both the benefits and the costs of permanent coverage.

clientProfiles.name: Robert Chen
clientProfiles.summary: Co-owner of a profitable manufacturing company with one partner. Most of his wealth is tied up in the business. He owns a 15-year-old whole life policy.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Spouse; two adult children who do not work in the business

facts.label: Business
facts.value: Owns 50% of a company with partner Lisa; no buy-sell agreement yet

facts.label: Existing coverage
facts.value: $250,000 whole life policy bought 15 years ago, with significant cash value

facts.label: Estate
facts.value: Mostly illiquid: business interest and real estate

clientProfiles.goal: Make sure his family receives fair value for his business interest and that Lisa can keep running the company if he dies.

decisions.prompt: What is the best way to handle the business interest at Robert's death?

options.text: A buy-sell agreement between Robert and Lisa, funded with life insurance on each owner
options.feedback: A funded buy-sell agreement guarantees a buyer, a price and the cash — Lisa keeps the business and Robert's family receives fair value.

options.text: Leave the business interest to his children in his will
options.feedback: The children do not work in the business; they could end up owning half of a company they cannot run, with no cash.

options.text: Key person insurance on Robert only, owned by the company
options.feedback: Key person coverage helps the company survive his loss, but it does not by itself buy his interest from his family.

decisions.prompt: With two owners, how should the buy-sell agreement be structured?

options.text: Either a cross-purchase plan (2 policies) or an entity plan (2 policies) — both work with two owners
options.feedback: With two owners, cross-purchase needs n × (n − 1) = 2 policies and an entity plan needs 2. The choice depends on other planning and tax advice.

options.text: A cross-purchase plan requiring four policies
options.feedback: Two owners need only 2 × 1 = 2 cross-purchase policies.

options.text: No insurance; the company can borrow the money when needed
options.feedback: Borrowing after an owner's death may be difficult or expensive; insurance provides cash when it is needed.

decisions.prompt: Another producer suggests surrendering Robert's old whole life policy to help pay for new coverage. Under New York rules, what must happen?

options.text: Treat it as a replacement: complete the Definition of Replacement and IMPORTANT Notice, give a Disclosure Statement explaining why the existing policy can't meet his objectives, and evaluate whether replacement is in his best interest
options.feedback: Surrendering existing coverage as part of buying new insurance is a replacement under Reg 60 (11 NYCRR 51.2), with required forms (51.5). Reg 187 (11 NYCRR 224.4) requires considering surrender charges, a new contestable period, lost benefits and his health rating before recommending it.

options.text: Surrender it first, then apply for the new policy later so no forms are needed
options.feedback: If the surrender is part of the transaction, it is still a replacement; splitting the steps to avoid the rules is improper.

options.text: Keep the existing policy and buy additional coverage for the buy-sell need
options.feedback: Keeping the existing policy avoids replacement and preserves its cash value and older incontestable status; this is often reasonable, though it still needs a suitability review.

decisions.prompt: What extra benefit could permanent coverage give Robert's estate?

options.text: Liquidity so his heirs can pay debts and settlement costs without selling real estate quickly
options.feedback: His estate is mostly illiquid; life insurance provides cash at death for estate conservation.

options.text: Guaranteed investment returns higher than the business
options.feedback: Insurance is not an investment guarantee; overstating returns would be a misrepresentation.

options.text: Protection against all estate settlement costs regardless of the amount
options.feedback: Coverage helps only to the extent of the face amount purchased.

takeaways: Buy-sell agreements funded by life insurance give surviving owners control and heirs fair cash value.
Cross-purchase needs n × (n − 1) policies; entity plans need one per owner.
In New York, using an existing policy's values to fund a new one is a replacement under Reg 60 and must be in the client's best interest under Reg 187.
Life insurance supplies liquidity for illiquid estates.

clientProfiles.name: Dorothy Malone
clientProfiles.summary: A retired widow on a fixed income who wants to cover her funeral and leave a small gift to her grandchildren.

facts.label: Income
facts.value: $2,600 per month from Social Security and a small pension

clientProfiles.goal: Make sure her children don't have to pay for her funeral, and leave a modest amount to her grandchildren.

decisions.prompt: Before recommending anything, what must the producer do under New York's best-interest regulation?

options.text: Make reasonable efforts to obtain her suitability information — income, budget, assets, existing coverage, goals, liquidity needs and willingness to accept non-guaranteed elements
options.feedback: 11 NYCRR 224.4(d) requires reasonable efforts to obtain suitability information before recommending; 224.3(g) lists the kinds of information.

options.text: Recommend the product with the highest commission and document it later
options.feedback: Only the consumer's interests may be considered; compensation must not influence the recommendation (224.4(b)(1)).

options.text: Ask only her age and health, since she wants a small policy
options.feedback: Age and health matter for underwriting, but best interest also requires understanding her budget, assets and goals.

decisions.prompt: Dorothy likes a policy whose premium would take nearly all of her $120 monthly cushion. What is the best course?

options.text: Recommend a smaller face amount or lower-cost design she can comfortably afford
options.feedback: A producer may not recommend a transaction without a reasonable basis to believe the consumer can meet its financial commitments (11 NYCRR 224.4(g)).

options.text: Sell the larger policy, since she wants it
options.feedback: Recommending coverage she likely cannot keep paying for is not in her best interest and risks a lapse.

options.text: Suggest she use part of her $30,000 savings to pay premiums
options.feedback: Using savings may be reasonable if it fits her liquidity needs, but it must be weighed against her need for emergency funds.

decisions.prompt: A competing salesperson's card reads 'Certified Senior Retirement Specialist' — a title he gave himself. What should Dorothy's producer understand about this?

options.text: Using a self-conferred senior designation is prohibited in New York
options.feedback: 11 NYCRR 225.2(a)(2)(ii) prohibits nonexistent or self-conferred senior-specific certifications; a violation is an unfair or deceptive practice (225.3).

options.text: Any senior title is fine as long as the agent is licensed
options.feedback: A license does not make a misleading senior designation permissible.

options.text: It is only a problem if Dorothy complains
options.feedback: The prohibition applies to the use itself, whether or not anyone complains.

takeaways: Recommend only coverage the client can reasonably afford to keep.
Self-conferred or misleading senior designations are prohibited (Reg 199).
